item.title: Emigrating from Switzerland: what happens to taxes after departure
item.description: After leaving Switzerland in May 2025, the payment of taxes does not always end. Here is what the legislation provides for those who move abroad.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - After emigration, taxes are normally paid only in the new country of residence - Exceptions: diplomatic staff, digital nomads and those who continue to earn income in Switzerland - Liability for less than one year: taxation based on income from 1 January to the day of departure
## Key facts - **What**: Obligation to pay taxes after emigrating from Switzerland - When: May 2025 (source date) - Where: Switzerland and new country of residence - Who: People moving abroad, diplomatic staff, digital nomads, seconded workers - Amount: Not yet specified (depends on the new country of residence)
## The complex tax issue after moving abroad
According to what was communicated in May 2025, those who leave Switzerland cannot always consider their tax obligations concluded. In fact, Swiss legislation provides for significant exceptions that maintain a fiscal link with the country even after moving abroad. This aspect, often underestimated, can reserve surprises for those preparing to embark on an emigration journey.
The general rule is simple: anyone who emigrates and works or receives an AVS income abroad is no longer subject to taxation in Switzerland, but exclusively in the new country of residence. However, as highlighted in the source, there are specific categories that continue to be subject to Swiss taxes. These include diplomatic staff, employees of international organizations and seconded workers from companies based in Switzerland. Digital nomads and those who keep income in Switzerland must also pay particular attention.
### Subjugation of less than one year: what changes
A crucial aspect concerns the situation of those who move abroad during the tax year. In these cases, Switzerland applies the so-called "subjugation of less than one year". This means that the taxable income is calculated based on the income actually received from January 1st until the day of the departure notification. For the taxable assets, however, reference is made to the balance sheet at the end of the tax period. It is a mechanism that aims to guarantee fair taxation even for those who do not spend the entire calendar year in Switzerland.
### The procedures to follow before leaving Switzerland
Before undertaking the transfer, it is essential to promptly submit the tax return for the current year, duly completed. This allows the tax office of the municipality of residence to correctly calculate the taxes due. As Urs Neuenschwander, communications manager at the Finance Directorate of the Canton of Zurich, points out, "it is recommended to contact the tax office at least 30 days before the date of the move abroad, after having consulted the website of the municipality of residence".
Another mandatory step concerns the appointment of a representative domiciled in Switzerland or the provision of a delivery address. The legislation varies depending on the cantons: in some cases it is necessary to pay all the taxes due before departure, while in others, such as the Canton of Bern, it is possible to pay the amount indicated on the tax statement from the new domicile abroad. As Dominik Rothenbühler, press officer of the Cantonal Tax Administration of the Canton of Bern, explains, «the Tax Administration sends the documents with the tax procedure to the delivery address provided and then, during the tax process, also the tax statement».
### The risks of leaving without resolving tax issues
Leaving Switzerland without having fulfilled your tax obligations can lead to serious consequences. The credit in favor of the authorities remains in existence and, in case of non-payment, there is a risk of credit recovery procedures even from abroad. This aspect underlines the importance of addressing every requirement before departure, thus avoiding future complications.
For those looking for official information, the Confederation provides resources on the website of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA). Further support can be provided by the Organization of the Swiss Abroad (OSA), which offers specific consultancy services for those living outside national borders.
### Why this aspect is relevant for those living in Switzerland
The complexity of Swiss tax rules does not stop at national borders. For anyone considering a move abroad, understanding these dynamics is essential to avoid surprises and ensure a smooth transition. Accurate planning and compliance with procedures are essential steps for those who wish to close their tax relationship with Switzerland correctly and without risks.

Practical guides on emigration and life abroad are available on the Frontaliere Ticino website, as well as useful tools to best tackle this journey. A concrete example is the page dedicated to emigration, which offers ideas and insights on the most relevant aspects of this life choice. ## The exceptions to the general rule: those who remain subject to Switzerland
Although the general rule states that those who emigrate from Switzerland pay taxes exclusively in the new country of residence, there are specific categories that remain subject to Swiss taxation. These exceptions, as indicated in the source, concern in particular:
- Swiss diplomatic personnel abroad, who continue to be subject to Swiss tax legislation; - Employees of international organizations based in Switzerland; - Workers posted by Swiss companies; - Persons who maintain income in Switzerland, regardless of their domicile; - Digital nomads with permanent ties to Swiss territory.
These categories must therefore pay particular attention to their tax situation, even after leaving the country. In many cases, in fact, Switzerland retains the right to tax income generated in Swiss territory, regardless of the place of residence of the interested party.
### Comparison between complete subjection and subjection of less than one year
An often overlooked aspect concerns the difference between those who move abroad permanently and those who spend only part of the year abroad. In the first case, taxation takes place exclusively in the new country of residence, while in Switzerland you no longer pay anything. In the second case, however, the regime of tax liability for less than one year applies, which entails partial taxation in Switzerland.
For example, for those who move in June, the taxable income will be calculated from January 1st to the day of departure. This means that if you receive income even after the move, it may be subject to taxation both in Switzerland and in the new country of residence, unless there is a double taxation agreement. A second crucial aspect concerns the appointment of a tax representative in Switzerland or the communication of a delivery address. The legislation varies depending on the cantons: in some cases, such as in Zurich, it is necessary to contact the tax office at least 30 days before departure. In others, such as the Canton of Bern, it is possible to receive and pay taxes from abroad as long as a valid delivery address has been provided.
### The consequences of a hasty departure
Anyone who decides to move abroad without having fulfilled their tax obligations runs the risk of leaving unpaid debts. In these cases, the credit in favor of the Swiss authorities remains in existence and can be recovered even after departure. This can lead to bureaucratic complications, penalties and, in some cases, the impossibility of obtaining tax certificates necessary for future operations, such as purchasing a house abroad or applying for visas.

The Federal Council is planning to significantly strengthen the banking supervisory authority. The aim is to equip Switzerland with control tools that other international financial centres already use, especially following the collapse of Credit Suisse (CS) three years ago. The proposal provides that the Federal Financial Market Supervisory Authority (Finma) can impose financial penalties and, just as importantly, make public the identities of banks that do not comply with the rules.
### An evolution marked by crises The history of Swiss banking regulation is not linear. Already in 1916 there was a draft federal law, but it remained unused until the crisis of the 1930s. The need to act became pressing after the failure of the Banque de Genève in 1931 and the crisis of the Swiss People's Bank, which in 1933 required intervention ## Analysis of the impact on financial stability The introduction of financial penalties and transparency on defaults marks a paradigm shift for the Swiss banking ecosystem. To date, Finma's lack of direct sanctioning powers has limited its ability to take prompt action on irregularities. If such instruments had been available earlier, it would have been possible to shed more light on the issues that led to the collapse of Credit Suisse.
### Comparison of old and new supervisory powers To understand the qualitative leap, it is useful to analyze what concretely changes for financial institutions operating in Switzerland:

The KKV has determined that takeovers must be authorized if they meet the following requirements:

item.description: Registrations fell by 3.2% in July, but electrification continues. BYD overtakes Tesla in the Swiss electric car market.

## In brief - New car sales down 3.2% in July 2026. - Total of 19,000 new registrations in Switzerland. - Alternative propulsion systems account for 76% of the market share. - BYD overtakes Tesla in electric car sales.
## Key Facts - **What**: Trend of the Swiss automotive market - When: July 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Auto-Switzerland - Amount: 3.2% decrease compared to the previous July
The Swiss car market slowed down in July 2026, following a brief recovery in June. According to data provided by the importers' association Auto-Switzerland, 19,000 fresh cars were put on the road, a decrease of 3.2% compared to the same period of the previous year. Despite this decline in overall volumes, the transition to greener engines continues to consolidate, profoundly influencing the choices of Swiss consumers.
### The growth of the electricity sector The detailed analysis for July reveals that alternative powertrains, which include electric, hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles, achieved an overall market share of 76%, up sharply from 68% in July 2025. At the heart of this dynamic is the regular hybrid segment, which holds a 37% share, up from 35% a year earlier. The purely electric sector also shows considerable vigor, reaching 26% of the market, with 4500 cars registered and a growth of 20% on an annual basis. At the same time, plug-in hybrid stands at 14%, compared to 12% previously. On the contrary, traditional engines are losing ground: petrol cars are down to 18% from 24% last year, while diesel vehicles are down to 6% from the original 8%. This shift towards environmentally friendly technologies is the direct result of an aggressive commercial strategy by manufacturers, who offer a wide range in different price ranges, while ensuring improved ranges and reduced operating costs. The director of Auto-Switzerland, Thomas Rücker, emphasizes that this electrification is a gradual process, actively supported by importers despite the economic challenges, which remain, according to the executive, "immense". Analyzing the cumulative data for the first seven months of 2026, the picture of the Swiss market appears more complex. Overall, 135,500 cars were registered, an increase of 2.1% compared to the same period in 2025. This reflects the resilience of the sector over the long term, despite monthly fluctuations. Looking at the specific volumes by type of propulsion, it can be seen that hybrids reached 49,600 units (+2%), while electric cars stood at 32,900 units (+20%). On the contrary, classic engines suffered: petrol vehicles fell to 28,600 units (-13%) and diesels to 7600 (-23%). Plug-in hybrids closed the period with 16,900 registrations (+21%). Of particular note is the increase in the share of 4x4 vehicles, from 50% to 53%, confirming a Swiss consumer preference for all-wheel drive.
### The challenge between BYD and Tesla Perhaps the most striking figure of this period is the rise of the Chinese manufacturer BYD. In the brand comparison, BYD sold 3300 vehicles between January and July, marking a growth of 1197% compared to 300 units in the same period of 2025. Tesla, while maintaining a growth of 2% over the seven months, experienced a decidedly difficult month of July with only 100 cars sold (-78%), against BYD's 600. This competition reflects a profound shift in Swiss market preferences, where new international players are rapidly eroding market share from established leaders. Volkswagen remains the leading brand with 15,300 cars sold, followed by Skoda (12,900), BMW (11,200) and Mercedes (10,700). Regulatory pressure remains a sticking point: Auto-Switzerland continues its battle against overregulation, calling on politicians to improve the regulatory framework to strengthen the engine of the economy. Importers remain focused on optimizing the offer, trying to meet the needs of customers who are increasingly attentive to operating costs and environmental performance, in a macroeconomic context that requires constant adaptation and technological innovation to maintain competitiveness on national markets.

item.description: The Swiss bicycle rental company Publibike is majority-owned by British investor Visionedgeone.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Publibike switches to Visionedgeone - Markus Bacher remains CEO and minority shareholder - Visionedgeone owns Inurba Mobility
## Key Facts - **What**: Majority transfer of Publibike to Visionedgeone - When: July 30, 2024 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Visionedgeone - Amount: Not specified
BERN - Swiss bicycle rental company Publibike is passing a majority stake to British investor Visionedgeone. Current CEO Markus Bacher will retain leadership of the company and will remain a minority shareholder. The news was reported on Monday by the CH-Media Group's "Schweiz heute" portal, after the same company had already announced the change of ownership on July 30 on its website. The price of the transaction was not disclosed.
With the transaction, the current shareholders are selling their shares, with the exception of Bacher. Among those retiring is Bern entrepreneur Thomas Binggeli, founder and owner of Thömus, who has said he wants to return to focusing fully on his other activities.
Visionedgeone has made a long-term commitment, for at least five years, Bacher indicated. The investor already owns Inurba Mobility, a bike sharing operator active in several European countries including France, Finland and Poland. The aim is to exploit possible synergies in terms of technology, distribution and management.
Under the new ownership, Publibike intends to strengthen investments in the fleet, services and technology, as well as expand the offer to other Swiss cities and municipalities. Currently, the company operates around 10,500 bicycles and e-bikes in around 120 cities and municipalities spread across ten cantons, with customers including Zurich, Bern, Basel, Biel and Aarau.
The public sector partly supports the business through annual contributions and guarantees to cover the deficit. Publibike was previously controlled by Swiss Post and was sold in 2022 to a group of investors led by Bacher, Binggeli and IT entrepreneur Guido Honegger. Since 2024, the company has been recording positive operating results (EBITDA), according to Bacher. ### Implications for the Swiss market
The acquisition of Publibike by Visionedgeone could lead to a strengthening of the bike sharing sector in Switzerland. With Visionedgeone's experience in several European countries, it is expected that Publibike will benefit from new technologies and better management practices. This could result in a more efficient service and greater geographical coverage, with potential new customers in other Swiss cities and municipalities.
### Synergies and innovation
The goal of leveraging technology and management synergies could lead to significant innovations in the industry. Visionedgeone, with its expertise in France, Finland, and Poland, could introduce new technology solutions that improve user experience and fleet management. This could include improvements in rental apps, more efficient charging systems for e-bikes, and new ways of distribution.
### Expansion and investment
With plans to expand its offerings to other Swiss cities and municipalities, Publibike could see a significant increase in its user base. This could lead to increased demand for bicycles and e-bikes, further stimulating the bike-sharing market. Investments in the fleet and services could also improve the quality of service offered, making Publibike an even more attractive choice for consumers.

The aim was to test whether Switzerland was doing enough to prevent the import of goods produced by forced labour. The International Labour Organization defines forced labour as "any work or service extorted from a person under threat of punishment and for which the person has not volunteered himself". Punishments may include violence, intimidation, or forms of coercion such as withholding wages or confiscating passports.

The Swiss tax landscape for the year 2026 remains complex, with a division of competences that sees the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV) define the general principles, while the individual cantons retain the right to set their own rates. This cantonal autonomy generates significant differences in the overall tax burden for taxpayers. In the Canton of Vaud, as in other cantons, the system is based on income brackets that determine the progression of the tax. It is essential to underline that for cross-border workers, withholding tax is the standard method of levy, withheld directly by the employer in Switzerland. This mechanism avoids double taxation, thanks to the tax credit provided for by the EC framework of 730 in Italy. The current legislation, including the management of the New Cross-Border Workers' Agreement which came into force on 1 January 2024, defines the applicable exemptions: 7,500 euros for 'old' cross-border workers, under a transitional regime until 2033, and 10,000 euros for new hires. The double taxation agreement between Italy and Switzerland, signed on 9 December 1976, remains the fundamental pillar of this cross-border balance. The calculation of the tax does not depend on institutions such as the FSIO, which is responsible for social security, but follows the directives of the cantonal administrations. ### Cantonal tax dynamics The discrepancy between the cantons arises not only from the basic rates, but also from the municipal multipliers that are added to the cantonal tax. In the canton of Vaud, the competent authorities regularly update the tables based on the parameters defined by the FTA/ESTV. item.description: Tens of thousands of migrants have crossed the border into the Schengen area. The episode inflames the political debate, even in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Tens of thousands of migrants have crossed the border into the Schengen area. - The incident is fueling political debate, even in Switzerland. - The Federal Council must introduce systematic border controls.
## Key facts - **What**: Massive influx of migrants into the Schengen area. - When: Thursday, March 17, 2023. - Where: Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, North Africa. - Who: Swiss Federal Council, Spanish Guardia Civil. - Amount: Around 49,000 arrivals in Ceuta and hundreds in Melilla.
The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa are under pressure from a massive influx of migrants. On Thursday, thousands of people reached Ceuta by swimming or walking from Morocco, thus entering the Schengen area, which also includes Switzerland. On Friday, the Spanish Guardia Civil reported 49,000 arrivals, not counting the hundreds of migrants who entered Melilla. The government has sent the army for support.
The causes are not yet fully clear. There is talk of a decision by the Spanish Supreme Court that migrants attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla by swimming cannot be turned back without further reasons. There is also speculation about a possible deliberate easing of controls by Morocco.
In Switzerland, the events in North Africa are sparking very different reactions politically.
"No one should risk their life to be protected"
Socialist National Councillor Michelle Dünki-Bättig speaks of shocking images: "People are trying to swim to a European border and dying in the attempt." She argues that the army and fences do not solve the problem; instead, they make escape routes even more dangerous. Europe needs safe and legal access routes and an effective sea rescue system.
Switzerland must also act, adds Dünki-Bättig. She calls for the reintroduction of asylum in embassies, abolished in 2012, which allowed asylum applications to be submitted at a Swiss representation abroad. The humanitarian visa, she says, is not an equivalent substitute: "No one who needs protection should have to risk their life just to apply for asylum."
"They are not refugees at all"
"What is happening is absolutely alarming," says Pascal Schmid, the SVP's asylum spokesman. "Whoever crosses the border in Ceuta is, in fact, also in Switzerland," referring to the Schengen and Dublin areas, where there are no systematic internal border controls to stop irregular migration. For this reason, he supports the request of the Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to suspend the Schengen agreement with Spain.
Schmid demands immediate measures: "The Federal Council must introduce systematic border controls immediately, as the SVP has been demanding for a long time." An "illegal mass migration" like in 2015 must be avoided at all costs, and the population must be protected from further imported crime. The democentric National Councillor and former judge also criticizes the "out-of-this-world" ruling of the Spanish court and denounces increasing legalization in the field of migration: "Intrusive justice disempowers politics, reducing its scope for action more and more."
"They are not refugees at all," Schmid reiterates. In the last session, the National Council established that the Maghreb states – Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia – must be considered safe countries of origin. Tens of thousands of unfounded applications, he argues, turn asylum law into a farce: "Once here, it takes a huge effort to expel them."
"Young people need a perspective"
Marc Jost, a National Councillor for the Evangelical People's Party of Switzerland (EVP), also criticizes the current approach: "The events in Ceuta clearly show that the combination of fences and general financial aid does not bring stability." It has not reduced migratory pressure or offered prospects to people on the spot. He proposes a two-pillar model, inspired by Swiss migration partnerships.
Firstly, a binding readmission agreement is needed for people without a right of residence: "Only a reliable procedure can combat trafficking networks and ensure the rule of law," says Jost. Secondly, EU funds should not be used for general aid but for concrete projects that create job and training opportunities.
### Implications for Switzerland
The events in Ceuta and Melilla have reopened the debate on border management and immigration in Switzerland. The need for systematic border controls has been raised by several political parties, including the SVP, which is calling for immediate measures to prevent "illegal mass migration."
Socialist National Councillor Michelle Dünki-Bättig, on the other hand, argues that Europe needs safe and legal access routes and an effective sea rescue system. She calls for the reintroduction of asylum in embassies, abolished in 2012, to allow people to submit asylum applications at a Swiss representation abroad.
Marc Jost, a National Councillor for the Evangelical People's Party of Switzerland (EVP), proposes a two-pillar model, inspired by Swiss migration partnerships. Firstly, a binding readmission agreement is needed for people without a right of residence. Secondly, EU funds should be used for concrete projects that create job and training opportunities.

## Key facts - **What**: Contractual rights for part-time work. - When: In force with current legislation. - Where: Swiss Confederation. - Who: SECO, AFC/ESTV, BFS. - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee, AD 1.1%.
Part-time work in Switzerland is governed by a regulatory framework that guarantees equal treatment with full-time employees. According to the SECO directives, the employment contract must clearly specify the employment rate and the expected tasks. For frontier workers, it is essential to remember that income tax at source is withheld only in Switzerland, while Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit in the EC framework of model 730. The new Frontier Agreement, signed on 23 December 2020 and entered into force on 1 January 2024, defines the current framework. It is essential to point out that Switzerland is not an EU/EEA member, which implies an autonomous management of employment relations. Reference bodies for social security and taxes, such as the AFC/ESTV for taxation and the FOPH/BAG for health, operate according to federal and cantonal laws ### Contractual and Pension Implications
Working part-time in Switzerland allows you to benefit from paid leaves and permits in proportion to your level of employment. A part-time employee with a 50% contract will enjoy the same rights in percentage terms as a full-time colleague. In the area of pension insurance, the second pillar (LPP/BVG) follows age bands and contributions that vary from 7% to 18%. It is crucial to monitor the payment of contributions, as these directly affect future income. Regarding the tax regime, frontalieri must manage their tax declaration in Italy using the tax credit to avoid double taxation, in accordance with the Convention against Double Taxation signed on December 9, 1976. For 'old' frontalieri, active before July 17, 2023, a 7,500 euro exemption is provided in the transitional regime 2024–2033, while for 'new' frontalieri the franchise is set at 10,000 euros. The calculation of net salary must consider mandatory deductions such as LAINF (accident insurance), which ranges from 0.7% to 1.5%. Those residing in Italy and working in Switzerland have the right to opt for LAMal (health insurance), with franchise rates varying between 300 and 2,500 CHF. It is not uncommon for the employer to request proof of insurance coverage. The difference between the regime before 2024 and the current one requires a careful review of the individual tax position with the Revenue Agency.
